thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why is TreeSet preferred over PriorityQueue for the enrolled students, but PriorityQueue preferred for the waitlist?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: Enrolled students need full sorted visibility and quick individual removal when any arbitrary student drops (TreeSet.remove is O(log N)). The waitlist only ever promotes the single top candidate (PriorityQueue.poll is O(log N)), which matches binary heap mechanics perfectly.

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: Why must the Student merit Comparator include studentId as a final tie-breaker?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: TreeSet considers two elements equal if comparator.compare(a, b) == 0. If two students have identical GPAs and credit hours, omitting the unique ID tie-breaker causes the TreeSet to discard the second student as a duplicate!

thinkBeforeYouCode.question: How does Set.containsAll() ensure prerequisite validation in O(K) time?
thinkBeforeYouCode.mentorInsight: Because completedCourses is a HashSet, probing each of the K prerequisites via contains() takes O(1) time, making the entire prerequisite check O(K) where K is the small number of course prerequisites.

activities.title: Practical Context: Airport Boarding Lounge & Standby Upgrade Queue
activities.description: How sorted sets and priority queues work in tandem at commercial airlines.
activities.content:
Consider an international first-class airline cabin with 10 seats. Passengers seated inside are arranged by loyalty tier and ticket value (TreeSet merit ranking). Once all 10 seats are booked, travelers seeking upgrades are placed on the standby upgrade list (PriorityQueue).

The standby list doesn't board in simple first-come-first-served order. A Platinum frequent flyer who requests an upgrade 1 hour before departure is prioritized above a Bronze flyer who requested it 3 days earlier (multi-tier priority heap). When a first-class passenger cancels their ticket, the automated system immediately polls the standby queue and issues a boarding pass to the top flyer.

This exact pattern governs enterprise university registration: TreeSets manage active merit-ranked seats, while PriorityQueues schedule waiting applicants.

activities.title: Architecture of Merit-Based Ranking and Priority Queues
activities.description: Technical analysis of TreeSet red-black trees and PriorityQueue binary min/max heaps.
activities.content:
### Formal Computer Science Definition
A priority scheduling system coordinates two distinct algebraic structures: a balanced binary search tree (`TreeSet`) maintaining a dynamically sorted view of active participants in $O(\log N)$ time, and a binary heap (`PriorityQueue`) providing $O(1)$ peek and $O(\log N)$ extract-max for prioritized scheduling.

### Dual Data Structure Coordination

```
                               CourseRegistrationEngine
                                          |
             +----------------------------+----------------------------+
             |                                                         |
   Enrolled (TreeSet<Student>)                                Waitlist (PriorityQueue<Entry>)
   - Red-Black Tree                                          - Binary Array Heap
   - Sorted: GPA desc -> Credits desc -> ID asc              - Priority: Seniority -> Timestamp asc
   - O(log N) insert, search, remove                         - O(1) peek(), O(log N) poll()
             |
             +--> Drop Event: enrolled.remove(student) -> enrolled.add(waitlist.poll())
```

### Key Contracts & Pitfalls
1. **TreeSet Invariant**: `TreeSet` uses `comparator.compare(a, b) == 0` for uniqueness! If two students have identical GPAs and credits, they will be treated as duplicate unless a unique field (like student ID) is appended to the comparator chain.
2. **PriorityQueue Invariant**: `PriorityQueue` does not maintain full sorted order; it guarantees only that the root element (head) has the highest priority.

questions.question: What happens if a TreeSet comparator compares only student GPA without an ID tie-breaker, and two students with GPA 3.8 are added?
options: Both students are stored side by side
The second student is rejected as a duplicate because compare(s1, s2) returns 0
The second student replaces the first student
questions.explanation: TreeSet defines set uniqueness using the Comparator contract. If compare(s1, s2) == 0, the set considers them identical elements and ignores the second addition.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of promoting a student from the PriorityQueue waitlist into the TreeSet enrolled roster?
options: O(log W + log E) where W is waitlist size and E is enrolled size
questions.explanation: Polling from the PriorityQueue requires re-heapifying in O(log W) time. Inserting into the TreeSet requires red-black tree insertion in O(log E) time. Total time is logarithmic O(log W + log E).

questions.question: Why is PriorityQueue preferred over a sorted ArrayList for the waitlist?
options: PriorityQueue uses less memory than ArrayList
PriorityQueue achieves O(log N) insertion while ArrayList requires O(N) element shifts to insert in sorted order
PriorityQueue guarantees total order across all elements
questions.explanation: Maintaining a sorted ArrayList requires O(N) shifts on insertion. A PriorityQueue binary heap inserts in O(log N) time, making it significantly more efficient for dynamic queues.

questions.question: How would you handle dynamic student GPA updates after they have already been inserted into the TreeSet?
questions.answer:
TreeSet does not monitor internal object mutations. If a student's GPA changes while inside the TreeSet, the node becomes misplaced in the red-black tree, corrupting tree invariants and future searches.

To update a student's GPA safely:
1. Remove the student from the TreeSet (enrolled.remove(student)) using their old state.
2. Update the student's GPA field.
3. Re-insert the student into the TreeSet (enrolled.add(student)).
This guarantees the red-black tree places the node at its new correct sorted position.

questions.question: Explain how you would prevent race conditions when thousands of students register concurrently at 9:00 AM.
questions.answer:
To protect course capacity from oversubscription under high concurrency:
1. Use an AtomicInteger for course seat reservations so threads can attempt seat reservation with decrementAndGet() before acquiring data locks.
2. Synchronize registration at the Course level using ReentrantLock so that admissions to the TreeSet and PriorityQueue occur atomically.
3. Use ConcurrentSkipListSet instead of TreeSet if lock-free concurrent sorted views are required.
